section.title: The Final Plague Foretold
section.sectionRationale: This short chapter is the tense pause before the terrible tenth plague. It explains why Pharaoh will not relent even now, gathers up the pattern of hardening across the whole plague cycle, and sets the stage for the Passover that follows.
section.thesis: The LORD announces the last and most severe plague in advance, promises to make a clear distinction between Egypt and Israel, and declares that Pharaoh's continued refusal serves His larger purpose of multiplying wonders and displaying His glory.
section.frameNote: Three short movements: the LORD tells Moses what is coming and what the people should ask of their neighbors; Moses proclaims the sentence to Pharaoh and leaves in anger; and a closing note explains why Pharaoh still would not listen.

units.label: The last plague and the plunder

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “I will bring upon Pharaoh and Egypt one more plague. After that, he will allow you to leave this place. And when he lets you go, he will drive you out completely.
Now announce to the people that men and women alike should ask their neighbors for articles of silver and gold.”
And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, Moses himself was highly regarded in Egypt by Pharaoh's officials and by the people.

units.label: Moses declares the sentence
units.note: the death of the firstborn, and a distinction made

verses.text: So Moses declared, “This is what the LORD says: ‘About midnight I will go throughout Egypt,

and every {{firstborn|firstborn}} son in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill, as well as the firstborn of all the cattle.
Then a great cry will go out over all the land of Egypt. Such an outcry has never been heard before and will never be heard again.

But among all the Israelites, not even a dog will snarl at man or beast.’ 
Then you will know that the LORD makes a {{distinction|distinction}} between Egypt and Israel.

And all these officials of yours will come and bow before me, saying, ‘Go, you and all the people who follow you!’ After that, I will depart.” 
And hot with anger, Moses left Pharaoh's presence.

units.label: The LORD's purpose in the hardening

verses.text: The LORD said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that My wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.”
Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, but the LORD {{hardened|hardened}} Pharaoh's heart so that he would not let the Israelites go out of his land.

firstborn.gloss: The firstborn, the son who held the place of honor, inheritance, and household headship. Striking the firstborn of Egypt answers Pharaoh's earlier order to kill Israel's infant sons, and it exposes every false god of Egypt at the point of life and death.

distinction.gloss: To set apart, to make a marked difference. The LORD does not merely spare Israel by chance; He deliberately distinguishes His covenant people from Egypt, a pattern that culminates in the blood on the doorframes in the next chapter.

hardened.gloss: To make strong, firm, or stubborn. Across Exodus, Pharaoh hardens his own heart and the LORD hardens it; both are true, and by this point in the story Pharaoh's own settled defiance has become the very means of God's judgment and glory.

basic.context: This chapter is the calm before the storm. God tells Moses what is about to happen, the last and worst of the ten plagues, before Moses even goes back in to Pharaoh. It reads like a script written ahead of time because it is: the outcome was never in doubt.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage describes real historical events, the announcement of the tenth plague and Israel's favor with the Egyptians. It is not a pattern for how to treat other nations today; the plunder of Egypt was a specific act of God's justice against a specific oppressor, later described in Scripture as wages finally paid to slaves who had earned them.
basic.originalLanguages: The word for firstborn, bekor, marks out the son of highest standing, so the plague strikes Egypt where its household order and even its gods are most exposed. God says He will make a palah, a distinction, between Egypt and Israel; and the LORD chazaq, hardens, Pharaoh's heart one final time before the last plague falls.
basic.typology: The death of the firstborn, spared only where blood marks the door in the very next chapter, foreshadows the substitution at the heart of the gospel: a life given so that another life is spared. Every firstborn in Egypt who dies without a substitute anticipates why every family in Israel needs a lamb.
basic.christ: This chapter has no direct messianic statement, but it sets up the next: judgment falling on every house without a covering, met only by the blood of a substitute. That is the logic of the cross, where Christ, our Passover, is sacrificed so that judgment passes over His people.
basic.god: God is patient, giving fair warning even of His final judgment, yet He is also just and unrelenting once patience is exhausted. He is also sovereign even over a hard human heart, ruling Pharaoh's continued defiance so that His power and His care for Israel are put on full display.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 12:29-30 carries out exactly what is announced here. Romans 9:17-18 uses Pharaoh to show God's sovereign purpose in judgment and mercy. 1 Corinthians 5:7 calls Christ our Passover lamb, the substitute this chapter's coming plague requires.
basic.oneStory: Egypt stands under a righteous sentence it cannot escape by its own power, and only a substitute will spare the firstborn. That pattern, judgment coming and a lamb standing in the gap, threads through the whole Bible and lands at the cross, where Christ becomes the firstborn who dies so that many are spared.

context.literary:
Exodus 11 is short, but it is carefully built. It falls into three movements: God's word to Moses, verses 1 to 3; Moses' word to Pharaoh, verses 4 to 8; and the narrator's summary, verses 9 and 10. The middle section is the only place in the plague cycle where the final judgment is announced in full before it falls, so the chapter works like a hinge, closing the nine plagues and opening the night of chapter 12.

The chapter seems to pick up where chapter 10 left off. Pharaoh had just said, "never see my face again," Exodus 10:28, and Moses had agreed. Yet in 11:4 Moses is still speaking to Pharaoh, and only in 11:8 does he leave "hot with anger." Many readers therefore take verses 1 to 3 as a pause in the scene, telling what God had already said to Moses, while verses 4 to 8 are Moses' last words in that same audience. The BSB footnote on verse 7 notes that some translators close the quotation at a different point, a reminder that the speeches here are tightly woven.

The key verb is "go out." God says, "I will go throughout Egypt," verse 4, literally "I am going out in the midst of Egypt." Pharaoh's officials will say, "Go, you and all the people," verse 8, and Moses answers, "After that, I will depart." Then "Moses left," verse 8. The same verb runs through all four clauses. God goes out in judgment, Israel goes out in freedom, and Moses goes out in anger. This is the verb that gives the exodus its name in later telling: "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt," Exodus 20:2.

The summary in verses 9 and 10 closes an inclusio. At the start God told Moses, "though I will multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, Pharaoh will not listen to you," Exodus 7:3-4. Now the narrator says the same thing, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that My wonders may be multiplied," verse 9, and "Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh," verse 10, echoing God's first charge in Exodus 4:21. What God said at the beginning has come true.
context.historical:
In the ancient world the firstborn son carried the future of a family. He received "a double portion of all that he has," Deuteronomy 21:17, and was called "the firstfruits of his father's strength." In Egypt the firstborn of Pharaoh was heir to a throne that claimed divine status. To strike the firstborn of every household was to strike the continuity of the nation, and to strike Pharaoh's firstborn was to strike the future of the god-king himself.

The range of verse 5 sweeps from the top of Egyptian society to the bottom: "from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill." Grinding grain by hand was the lowest labour, done by slave women and prisoners; Samson was forced to "grind grain in the prison," Judges 16:21, and Isaiah tells proud Babylon to "take millstones and grind flour," Isaiah 47:2, as a sign of humiliation. When the plague actually falls, the text uses a parallel extreme, "the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon," Exodus 12:29. No one in Egypt is too high or too low to be touched.

This judgment answers what Egypt had done. Pharaoh had ordered that every Hebrew son be thrown into the Nile, Exodus 1:22, and God had warned from the start, "Israel is My firstborn son... since you have refused to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son," Exodus 4:22-23. The tenth plague is not an arbitrary cruelty but the long-announced consequence of a policy of infanticide and a refusal to release God's son.

The request for silver and gold, verse 2, reflects the reality of slavery. Israel had worked for generations without wages. The law would later forbid sending a released slave away empty-handed: "furnish him liberally from your flock, your threshing floor, and your winepress," Deuteronomy 15:13-14, and it bases this on Israel's own memory of Egypt, Deuteronomy 15:15. The Egyptians' willing gifts were a kind of back pay. Verse 3 notes that Moses himself had become "highly regarded" in Egypt. The man who once fled Pharaoh in fear, Exodus 2:15, now stood before him with the respect of Pharaoh's own court.
context.canonical:
The tenth plague was announced long before chapter 11. God promised Abraham that He would judge the nation that enslaved his descendants and that "afterward they will depart with many possessions," Genesis 15:14. He told Moses at the burning bush that Israel would not leave "empty-handed" but would "plunder the Egyptians," Exodus 3:21-22, and He named the firstborn as the final target in Exodus 4:22-23. Chapter 11 gathers those promises into one speech, and chapter 12 fulfils them to the letter, Exodus 12:29-36.

Israel's memory of this night became permanent in law and worship. Every firstborn was consecrated to the LORD, and every firstborn son was to be redeemed, and each father was to explain why: "when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt," Exodus 13:15. The Levites were later taken "in place of every firstborn Israelite," Numbers 3:12-13. The psalms rehearse it: "He struck all the firstborn of Egypt," Psalm 78:51, and Psalm 136:10 sets it inside the refrain "His loving devotion endures forever." Israel sang of the tenth plague as an act of covenant love toward them.

The prophets could turn it around. Amos warns Israel of wailing in every street "for I will pass through your midst," Amos 5:17, echoing the words God used of Egypt in Exodus 12:12. A people that behaved like Egypt could face Egypt's night.

The silver and gold have a history of their own. Some of it was melted into the golden calf, Exodus 32:2-4, and some was given freely to build the tabernacle, Exodus 35:22. The same gifts could be turned to idolatry or to worship.

The New Testament draws on the chapter in several ways. Hebrews 11:28 says Moses kept the Passover "so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel's own firstborn." Paul uses Pharaoh's hardened heart to show God's freedom in mercy and judgment, Romans 9:17-18. Jesus is Mary's "firstborn," Luke 2:7, presented at the temple under the law of Exodus 13, Luke 2:22-23, and He is "the firstborn from among the dead," Colossians 1:18. Peter reminds believers they were redeemed "not with perishable things such as silver or gold" but "with the precious blood of Christ," 1 Peter 1:18-19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand that their deliverance would come entirely on God's terms and in God's time. The chapter announces the outcome before it happens, down to the hour, "about midnight," verse 4. Israel was to see that the exodus was not a lucky escape but a judgment carried out exactly as God had said, and to trust His word in every later crisis for that reason.

He wanted them to see the justice of the final plague. The chapter recalls, without needing to say it, that Egypt had tried to destroy Israel's sons, Exodus 1:22, and that God had warned Pharaoh about his own firstborn from the very beginning, Exodus 4:23. Israel was to understand that God is not capricious. He had spoken, waited through nine plagues, and given Pharaoh every opportunity to release His firstborn son.

He also wanted them to notice the distinction. The great cry of Egypt, verse 6, stands against the silence of Israel, where "not even a dog will snarl," verse 7. The difference was God's doing: "the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel." Israel was not spared because it was more righteous, as chapter 12 will make clear when even Israelite homes need the blood. It was spared because God chose to mark it as His own.

Finally, the summary of verses 9 and 10 was meant to answer the question every reader asks: why did it take so long? The answer is that God was multiplying His wonders. The delay was not failure but purpose.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter narrates a unique act of God's judgment and a unique provision for His people at the founding of Israel. It does not license anyone to take property from others, to punish nations by harming their children, or to treat enemies as God treated Egypt. Vengeance belongs to God, "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord," Romans 12:19, and the tenth plague is an example of that divine prerogative, not a model for human action.

Moses' anger in verse 8 is also described rather than commanded. It was an anger fitting to the moment, at a king who would bring death on his own people rather than yield. The New Testament allows such anger but guards it: "Be angry, yet do not sin," Ephesians 4:26.

What does carry forward is the principle behind the silver and gold. Israel's law turned this event into a rule of generosity: a freed slave must not be sent away empty-handed, Deuteronomy 15:13-15. God's people are to treat those who have served them with the same justice God showed Israel when He saw that its labour was paid.

debates.question: Was asking the Egyptians for silver and gold a form of deception?

views.label: A misleading request to borrow
views.case: Some older translations rendered the verb in verse 2 as "borrow," and critics have asked whether Israel took goods under false pretences, knowing they would not return. On this view the text records a questionable act that God permitted.

views.label: A legitimate request for gifts and wages
views.case: The Hebrew verb simply means "ask," and the text says the LORD gave the people favor so that the Egyptians "granted their request," Exodus 12:36. After generations of unpaid labour, what Israel received was closer to back pay than to a loan. Deuteronomy 15:13-15 later requires that freed slaves be sent away with generous gifts, and it grounds that rule in this very event.

views.label: The spoils of God's victory
views.case: Exodus 3:22 and 12:36 say that Israel "plundered" Egypt, the language of a victor stripping the defeated. On this view the gifts are the spoils of a war God fought and won, as Genesis 15:14 foretold. The Egyptians' willing giving is itself a sign that they have been defeated.

debates.bearing: The second and third views fit the text best and are not in tension. The Egyptians were not tricked; they gave willingly and knowingly, pressed by the plagues and moved by God's favor. The gifts were both wages owed to slaves and spoils won by the LORD, and Israel's own law turned the event into a rule of generosity.

debates.question: How does Moses' speech in 11:4-8 fit with Pharaoh's order in 10:28 that Moses never see his face again?

views.label: One continuous audience
views.case: On this reading 11:1-3 is a pause in the story, reporting what God had told Moses beforehand, and 11:4-8 continues the scene of 10:24-29 without a break. Moses answers Pharaoh's threat with the announcement of the tenth plague and then "left Pharaoh's presence," 11:8. He keeps his word in 10:29 and never seeks another audience.

views.label: A separate, later audience
views.case: Others take chapter 11 as a new occasion, with Moses returning to Pharaoh once more. On this reading 10:29 is Moses' agreement with Pharaoh's terms, not a vow, and the story does not stress the tension.

debates.bearing: The first reading explains why Moses leaves "hot with anger" at the end of 11:8 and why he never again goes to Pharaoh. When the two meet again in Exodus 12:31 it is because Pharaoh "summoned Moses and Aaron by night." The king who banned Moses from his face is the one who sends for him, and his last request is, "bless me also," Exodus 12:32.

study.originalLanguages:
The word God uses for the last plague in verse 1 is nega', from the verb naga', "to touch." It is literally "one more touch" or "stroke." The same word is used throughout Leviticus 13 for an infection on the skin that the priest must examine. The final judgment is described as a single touch of God's hand, as though after all the swarms and storms God needed only to reach out once.

Verse 1 also says Pharaoh "will drive you out completely." The Hebrew doubles the verb garash, "driving he will drive you out," the intensive construction that sets an infinitive beside the finite verb. God had promised in Exodus 6:1 that Pharaoh would "drive them out of his land," and Exodus 12:39 records that Israel was indeed "driven out of Egypt." It is the same verb used when God "drove out the man" from Eden, Genesis 3:24. There it meant exile from God's presence; here it means release into it.

In verse 2 the people are to "ask," sha'al, their neighbours for silver and gold. It is the ordinary verb for asking, and it gives no hint of trickery. The favor Israel received in verse 3 is chen, the word used when "Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD," Genesis 6:8. Behind the Egyptians' goodwill is the grace of God. Exodus 3:22 and 12:36 add that Israel "plundered" Egypt, using the verb natsal in a stem that means to strip. In its causative stem the same verb means to rescue, and it is the verb of God's promise in Exodus 3:8, "I have come down to rescue them." God rescues Israel from Egypt, and Israel strips Egypt on the way out, the same verb in two directions.

The key word of verse 5 is bekhor, "firstborn." It is related to bikkurim, the "firstfruits" of the harvest, Exodus 23:16, and both words express the idea that what comes first belongs in a special way to God. Psalm 105:36 uses a parallel image when it calls the firstborn of Egypt "the firstfruits of all their vigor."

The "great cry" of verse 6 is tse'aqah. It is the same word used when God said to Moses, "I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors," Exodus 3:7, and "the cry of the Israelites has reached Me," Exodus 3:9. The cry of the oppressed now becomes the cry of the oppressor. Exodus 12:30 fulfils it with the same word, translated "loud wailing."

Verse 7 contains a vivid idiom: "not even a dog will snarl," literally "not a dog will sharpen its tongue." The same idiom appears in Joshua 10:21, where "no one dared to utter a word against the Israelites." Nothing, not even an animal, will threaten Israel that night. The verse then says that "the LORD makes a distinction," using palah, the verb of Exodus 8:22 and 9:4. In Exodus 8:23 the BSB has "a distinction," but the Hebrew text as it stands there reads pedut, "redemption," though the Greek translators read "distinction": "I will put a redemption between My people and your people." The distinction God makes between Israel and Egypt is, at root, redemption, the same word family used for the redemption of the firstborn in Exodus 13:13.

Finally, "wonders" in verses 9 and 10 is mofet, the word paired with "signs" in Exodus 7:3 and Deuteronomy 6:22. The Greek translation regularly rendered it with teras, and that pairing lives on in the New Testament, where Jesus is "certified by God to you by miracles, wonders, and signs," Acts 2:22. And Moses' anger in verse 8 is literally "in the burning of the nose," the vivid Hebrew idiom for anger.

typology.type: The firstborn of Egypt and the firstborn Son of God
typology.fulfillment: Egypt's firstborn died because Pharaoh refused to release God's firstborn, Israel, Exodus 4:22-23. The New Testament names Jesus as the firstborn in a fuller sense: Mary's "firstborn" presented under the law of Exodus 13, Luke 2:22-23, the true Son called "out of Egypt," Matthew 2:15, and "the firstborn from among the dead," Colossians 1:18. The escalation is that God, who struck Egypt's firstborn in judgment, "did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all," Romans 8:32. The type falls short because Egypt's sons died for their father's sin, while Christ died willingly for the sins of others.

typology.type: Silver and gold, and the price of redemption, Exodus 11:2
typology.fulfillment: Israel left Egypt carrying silver and gold, a sign of God's victory and provision. Peter uses those very metals to describe what did not redeem the church: "it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed... but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot," 1 Peter 1:18-19. The escalation is from the wealth God's people carried out of slavery to the price God paid to bring them out. The type falls short because Egypt's gold could be melted into a calf, Exodus 32:4, while the blood of Christ cannot be turned to any other use.

typology.type: The distinction between Egypt and Israel, Exodus 11:7
typology.fulfillment: God said He would make a distinction, and in the Hebrew of Exodus 8:23 that distinction is called a redemption. On the night of the tenth plague the line fell between houses marked with blood and houses without it, Exodus 12:13. The New Testament speaks of God presenting Christ "as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood," Romans 3:25, and of believers "justified by His blood" and "saved from wrath through Him," Romans 5:9. The escalation is that the distinction is no longer ethnic but is drawn around all who are in Christ. The type falls short because Israel's distinction spared lives for one night; the redemption in Christ is eternal.

typology.type: The spoils of victory given to God's people
typology.fulfillment: The Egyptians gave Israel silver, gold and clothing, and the text calls it plunder, Exodus 12:36. Some of it later built the tabernacle, Exodus 35:22. Paul describes Christ's victory in similar terms, quoting Psalm 68: "When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men," Ephesians 4:8, and those gifts build up the church, Ephesians 4:11-12. At the cross Christ "disarmed the powers and authorities," Colossians 2:15. The type falls short because Egypt's plunder was material; the gifts of the risen Christ are people and graces for building God's dwelling.

study.christ:
Exodus 11 leads to Christ above all through the theme of the firstborn. From the start God called Israel "My firstborn son," Exodus 4:22, and the tenth plague is the contest between God's firstborn and Pharaoh's. Matthew sees Jesus as the true Israel when he applies Hosea 11:1 to the child brought back from Egypt: "Out of Egypt I called My Son," Matthew 2:15. Luke calls Him Mary's "firstborn," Luke 2:7, and records that His parents presented Him in the temple because "Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord," Luke 2:23, the very law that arose from the night announced in this chapter, Exodus 13:2 and 13:15. Paul calls Him "the firstborn over all creation" and "the firstborn from among the dead," Colossians 1:15 and 1:18, and says God's purpose is that He would be "the firstborn among many brothers," Romans 8:29.

The deepest connection is a reversal. In Egypt God struck the firstborn of His enemies to free His own people. At the cross God gave up His own firstborn to free His enemies. Paul says God "did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all," Romans 8:32. The sentence that fell on every unprotected house in Egypt fell on Christ, so that those who belong to Him are "saved from wrath through Him," Romans 5:9.

It leads to Christ through the language of going out. God says, "I will go throughout Egypt," and Israel goes out. On the mountain of transfiguration Moses himself appeared with Elijah and spoke with Jesus about "His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem," Luke 9:31. The Greek word for departure is exodos. The exodus Moses led was a shadow of the one Christ would accomplish through His death and resurrection.

It leads to Christ through the distinction God makes, which the Hebrew of Exodus 8:23 calls a redemption. In the next chapter it will be marked by the blood of a lamb. Paul says, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed," 1 Corinthians 5:7, and Peter says believers are redeemed "with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot," 1 Peter 1:19. The line between judgment and safety is drawn at the cross.

It also leads to Christ through the great cry. Egypt's night was filled with wailing. At the cross it was Jesus who "cried out in a loud voice," Matthew 27:46, taking into Himself the anguish that judgment brings, so that one day God will "wipe away every tear" from His people's eyes, Revelation 21:4.

These links are drawn by the New Testament itself. The chapter is not an allegory of the cross, but the story it begins is the story the cross completes.
study.god:
Exodus 11 shows a God who announces His judgment before He acts. After nine plagues He still does not strike without warning. He tells Moses exactly what will happen and when, and Moses tells Pharaoh. God's judgments are not ambushes. He speaks first, as He did with Noah, with Nineveh, and with Jerusalem, because He takes "no pleasure in the death of the wicked," Ezekiel 33:11.

He is just, and His justice fits the crime. Pharaoh tried to destroy Israel's sons, Exodus 1:22, and refused to release God's firstborn son, Exodus 4:23. The judgment falls on Egypt's firstborn. God warned about this from the very first message, and the tenth plague is the working out of what Pharaoh chose. Scripture does not hide that this is terrible. It calls the cry that follows unlike anything "heard before" or "again," verse 6. God's justice is not casual.

He is impartial. The judgment reaches "the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne" and "the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill," verse 5. God is the great and awesome God, "showing no partiality and accepting no bribe," Deuteronomy 10:17, and "God does not show favoritism," Romans 2:11. No rank protects and no poverty excuses. The whole nation that shared in the oppression shares in the judgment.

He is faithful to His people and cares about their wrongs. He gives Israel favor with the Egyptians and sees to it that they leave with silver and gold, fulfilling what He promised to Abraham centuries earlier, Genesis 15:14. The same God who "executes justice for the fatherless and widow," Deuteronomy 10:18, makes sure that slaves who were never paid do not leave empty-handed.

He is sovereign over the human heart, and His purposes cannot be frustrated. Verses 9 and 10 look back over the whole cycle and explain it: Pharaoh's refusal served God's purpose "so that My wonders may be multiplied." God does not merely react to Pharaoh. He governs the whole story, while holding Pharaoh responsible for every refusal.

He acts in person. "About midnight I will go throughout Egypt," verse 4. The final act of deliverance is not delegated. God Himself goes out in judgment and in rescue. That is why Israel's later confession of faith would begin, "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt," Exodus 20:2.

For worship, the chapter calls for fear and gratitude together: fear of a God whose word will surely come to pass, and gratitude that He has drawn a line of redemption around His people and taken the judgment on Himself in His Son.

crossReferences.note: "Israel is My firstborn son... since you have refused to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son!" The tenth plague was announced at the very start of Moses' mission. Exodus 11 is not a new idea but the long-delayed consequence of Pharaoh's refusal to release God's son.

At midnight the LORD struck every firstborn, "from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon," and there was loud wailing in Egypt. The announcement of Exodus 11:4-6 is fulfilled precisely, down to the hour and the extent.

God told Abram that his descendants would be enslaved and mistreated, but "I will judge the nation they serve as slaves, and afterward they will depart with many possessions." The silver and gold of Exodus 11:2 fulfil a promise made more than four centuries earlier.

A released slave must not be sent away empty-handed but furnished "liberally" from flock, threshing floor and winepress, because "you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you." The gifts of Exodus 11:2 become the model for Israel's own treatment of freed slaves.

When a son asks about the redemption of the firstborn, the father is to explain that the LORD killed every firstborn in Egypt when Pharaoh refused. The night announced in chapter 11 became the reason every Israelite firstborn belonged to God and had to be redeemed.

Amos warns of wailing in every street and vineyard, "for I will pass through your midst," words that echo God's passing through Egypt in Exodus 12:12. The prophet turns the tenth plague on an Israel that has come to behave like Egypt, showing that covenant status does not protect the unrepentant.

"By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel's own firstborn." Hebrews reads Moses' response to the announcement of Exodus 11 as an act of faith, trusting God's word about a judgment that had not yet fallen.

"He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all." In Egypt God struck the firstborn of His enemies to free His people. At the cross He gave up His own Son to free His enemies. The theme of the firstborn reaches its deepest point in this reversal.

Believers were redeemed "not with perishable things such as silver or gold" but with "the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot." Peter sets the silver and gold of the exodus against the blood of the Lamb, showing what the real price of redemption was.

Christ is "the beginning and firstborn from among the dead." The title that marked Egypt's sons for judgment marks Christ for supremacy. He is the firstborn who died and rose, so that death, which came for Egypt's firstborn, has been overcome in Him.

The gold earrings Israel carried out of Egypt were melted down into a calf, and the people said, "These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" The gifts God provided in Exodus 11 were quickly turned to idolatry, a warning that God's blessings can be misused.

Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about "His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem." The Greek word is exodos. Moses, who once announced the last plague before Israel's exodus, now speaks with Christ about the greater exodus of His death and resurrection.

study.oneStory:
The firstborn is one of the quiet threads of Genesis. Cain was the firstborn, and Abel's offering was accepted. Esau was the firstborn and "despised his birthright," Genesis 25:34. Jacob crossed his hands to put the younger Ephraim ahead of Manasseh, Genesis 48:17-19. Again and again God showed that His choice did not follow human rank. Then, in Exodus 4:22, He declared that the whole people of Israel was His "firstborn son." Exodus 11 is the moment when that claim is tested against the most powerful household on earth, and God's firstborn goes free while Egypt's dies.

The chapter also answers the cry that opened the book. Israel groaned and "cried out" under slavery, Exodus 2:23, and God heard. Now it is Egypt that cries, verse 6. The God who hears the oppressed is also the God who judges oppressors, and the reversal is complete.

But the rescue is not yet a clean victory for the righteous over the wicked. In chapter 12 Israel's firstborn will also be exposed to the destroyer unless the blood of a lamb marks their doors. The story sets up the Bible's great teaching that deliverance from judgment comes through a substitute. Every firstborn son in Israel from then on had to be redeemed, Exodus 13:13, as a living reminder that he owed his life to a death in his place.

That pattern comes to rest in Christ. He is God's firstborn and only Son, and instead of God's firstborn being spared while others die, God gives up His firstborn so that others may live, Romans 8:32. Those who belong to Him become "the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven," Hebrews 12:23, sharing the status He alone deserves.

The story ends where the tears of Egypt's night are no more. In the new creation God "will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain," Revelation 21:4. The silver and gold Israel carried out of Egypt are answered by the city into which "the glory and honor of the nations" will be brought, Revelation 21:26. The judgment announced in Exodus 11 was real, but it was not the last word. The last word is a city where the firstborn and all his brothers live forever in the presence of God.

quiz.q: What does the LORD announce to Moses at the start of this chapter?

options.text: One more plague is coming, after which Pharaoh will drive Israel out completely.
options.note: Verse 1 states this plainly; the outcome is settled before it happens.

options.text: Pharaoh has already agreed to release Israel for good.
options.note: Not yet; Pharaoh has broken his word repeatedly and will need this final plague.

options.text: The plagues are over and Israel should prepare to stay in Egypt.
options.note: The opposite is true; one final and decisive plague remains.

options.text: Moses should return to Midian for his own safety.
options.note: Nothing in the text suggests this; Moses stays to deliver the LORD's message.

quiz.q: What is the coming plague, and who is exempt?

options.text: The death of every firstborn in Egypt, but not even a dog will snarl among the Israelites.
options.note: Verses 5 to 7 describe exactly this, God's marked distinction between the two peoples.

options.text: A plague on all firstborn, Egyptian and Israelite alike.
options.note: Close, but it misses the crucial exemption for Israel that the passage emphasizes.

options.text: A plague only on Pharaoh's own household.
options.note: It reaches Pharaoh's throne, but strikes every Egyptian household, not his alone.

options.text: A plague of total darkness with no mention of the firstborn.
options.note: Darkness was the previous plague, chapter 10; this chapter announces the firstborn's death.

quiz.q: Why does Moses leave Pharaoh's presence hot with anger in verse 8?

options.text: He has just delivered the LORD's sentence of judgment on unrepentant, oppressive Pharaoh.
options.note: Moses speaks God's righteous anger at Pharaoh's persistent, cruel refusal to let Israel go.

options.text: Pharaoh has physically attacked Moses.
options.note: The text does not describe an attack; the anger flows from delivering the terrible verdict.

options.text: Moses is frustrated that God has not acted sooner.
options.note: The text gives no hint Moses is angry at God; his anger matches the moment with Pharaoh.

options.text: Moses regrets confronting Pharaoh at all.
options.note: There is no regret in the text; Moses delivers the message in full.

quiz.q: According to verse 9, why will Pharaoh not listen to Moses and Aaron?

options.text: So that the LORD's wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.
options.note: This is the LORD's own stated purpose in the continued hardening.

options.text: Because Moses spoke too harshly to him.
options.note: The text gives a theological reason, God's purpose, not a complaint about Moses' tone.

options.text: Because Pharaoh had not yet heard about the earlier plagues.
options.note: Pharaoh has seen nine plagues already; this misses the point of the verse.

options.text: There is no reason given in the text.
options.note: A reason is given directly: so that God's wonders would be multiplied.

quiz.q: How does this chapter set up the Passover in Exodus 12?

options.text: It announces the death of the firstborn that only the blood of a substitute lamb will avert.
options.note: This is exactly the problem chapter 12's Passover instructions solve.

options.text: It commands Israel to build an altar of unhewn stone.
options.note: That instruction belongs to Exodus 20, not to this chapter's setup for Passover.

options.text: It tells Israel to leave Egypt immediately, that same night.
options.note: The immediate departure comes later, after the plague falls in chapter 12; this chapter is the warning beforehand.

options.text: It has no connection to the Passover.
options.note: The connection is direct and deliberate; this chapter is the warning the Passover instructions answer.

questions: God gave fair warning before the final plague fell. Where in your life might God be giving you warning right now that you are tempted to ignore, the way Pharaoh did?

The LORD made a clear distinction between Egypt and Israel. What is it like to know that in Christ, God has made a similarly clear distinction for you, passing over judgment because of the blood of the Lamb?
Moses left Pharaoh's presence hot with anger at persistent injustice. Where do you need godly anger at oppression or cruelty, rather than passive tolerance of it?
God's patience with Pharaoh was real, but it was not endless. How does this shape the way you think about delayed consequences, either in your own life or in the world around you?
Every firstborn in Egypt needed a covering they did not have. What are you trusting to cover you before God, and is it anything less than the blood of Christ?

translationNotes.note: Highly regarded translates a phrase meaning Moses was great or esteemed in Egyptian eyes, a striking reversal from the earlier hostility of Pharaoh's court.
Not even a dog will snarl is an idiom for complete undisturbed safety, contrasting sharply with the great cry rising across Egypt in the same night.
Wonders here renders a word used throughout the plague cycle for signs that display God's power beyond ordinary explanation, distinct from the more general word for miracle.
